title: Rationalism and Divergent Sinomodernity
gist: Farrell Gregory argues that Bay Area rationalist forecasters wrongly expected China to nationalize AI and restrict open weights; instead Xi reaffirmed openness at WAIC 2026, and cheap Chinese open-weight models from DeepSeek and Moonshot are compressing US frontier lab pricing and moats. He attributes the misread to assumed shared utility functions and urges attention to China's contingent 'technical facts' such as labor structure and its existing cybersecurity state.

insights.claim: Xi Jinping's July 2026 World AI Conference speech, delivered the day after Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, reaffirmed China's commitment to open-source AI, undercutting Western expectations that China would abandon open weights as frontier costs rise.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Removes a widely assumed catalyst (Chinese open-weight shutdown) that would restore pricing power to US frontier labs.
insights.quote: “We should adhere to the principle of openness,” Xi said

insights.claim: Chinese AI strategy relies on billions of dollars of compute vouchers and small-firm support to sustain many labs releasing capable open-weight models, built with both novel methods and distillation from American frontier models, atop a churning layer of application-specialist firms.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: State subsidy of a fragmented open-weight ecosystem structurally pressures global model pricing.
insights.quote: Chinese labs and entrepreneurs have for the last few years pursued a strategy involving a multitude of labs releasing capable open-weight models

insights.claim: Chinese official AI documents since the 2017 Next Generation AI Development Plan frame AI in terms of industrial competitiveness, diffusion and self-sufficiency rather than a race to AGI; the AI+ Plan does not mention competition or America at all.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
entities: Next Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan
insights.so_what: Signals Chinese policy optimizes for broad economic diffusion, favoring cheap, widely deployed models over winner-take-all frontier bets.
insights.quote: The Chinese AI+ Plan doesn’t mention competition at all, nor does it even mention America.
insights.locator: This does not seem to be

insights.claim: US policy, by contrast, frames AI as a winner-take-all LLM-scaling race toward superintelligence, as in the 2025 AI Action Plan and a 2024 USCC call for a Manhattan Project-like AGI program.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
entities: U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission
insights.so_what: The asymmetry in national objectives drives different capex intensity and pricing behavior between US and Chinese labs.
insights.quote: “whoever has the largest AI ecosystem will set global AI standards and reap broad economic and military benefits.”

insights.claim: China can tolerate wide domestic access to highly capable open-weight models partly because the Cyberspace Administration of China already runs pre-deployment registration, continual security testing, and can unilaterally order model changes, as in a campaign that pushed Alibaba, Zhipu, MiniMax and DeepSeek to curb malicious code generation.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Existing state control reduces the perceived need for China to close weights, lowering odds of a policy reversal.
insights.quote: Generative AI models are subject to twin pre-deployment registration and review regimes.

insights.claim: The author expects Chinese AI governance to stay unchanged in the near term: widely distributed capable open-weight models, no nationalization of labs and no centralized Manhattan Project.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Investors should not underwrite US lab valuations on a near-term Chinese open-weight retreat.
insights.quote: No nationalization of the labs, and no Manhattan Project in Inner Mongolia, at least not yet.

insights.claim: Influential forecasts such as Leopold Aschenbrenner's "Situational Awareness" and the AI Futures Project's "AI 2027" predicted a Chinese 'wake-up' with nationalization of frontier research by mid-2026, which has not happened, as the AI 2027 authors themselves concede.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Widely used scenario models for AI geopolitics have a demonstrated blind spot on China, so positioning based on them is mispriced.
insights.quote: “we probably would have heard by now if the CCP had consolidated the various Chinese AI projects…in general it seems that ‘China Wakes Up’ has not yet happened.”
insights.locator: In a recent quarterly timeline update

insights.claim: Bay Area rationalism's habit of assuming different polities share similar utility functions for a technology at scale leads forecasters to downplay domestic political and cultural contingencies, causing systematic errors about China.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Forecasts built on coarse-grained mutual-rationality assumptions should be discounted when they predict foreign policy behavior.
insights.quote: Rationalists have an expectation that different people and polities will have similar utility functions for the same technology once it has reached sufficient scale.
insights.locator: There is a particular aspect of

insights.claim: Rationalist framing is heavily overrepresented among staff at major AI labs, safety evaluators and forecasting teams, so its biases propagate into mainstream AI policy discourse.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Lab and policy narratives share a common analytic monoculture, increasing correlated error in consensus views.

insights.claim: The author argues that America's past bet that Chinese economic liberalization would bring political liberalization caused deindustrialization and supply chain dependencies, and that repeating such misreadings in AI would be even more devastating.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Policy errors on China have historically created durable supply chain leverage against the US; AI could repeat this.
insights.quote: The result was the deindustrialization of America and the creation of countless supply chain reliances that are still used as leverage against the U.S. today.

insights.claim: Using Yuk Hui's distinction, the neural-network technology is a universal 'technical tendency', while existential-risk concern, fear of labor displacement and governance responses are contingent 'technical facts' that differ by culture; rationalist forecasts overweight tendencies and underweight facts.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A useful lens: expect convergent technology but divergent regulation and adoption between the US and China.
insights.quote: It seems that purely rationalist predictions of Chinese AI overestimate the technical tendencies and underestimate the technical facts.

insights.claim: Even if China eventually does change AI governance, timing matters enormously: a shift in two months versus two years produces very different outcomes, and China's reaction need not mirror America's.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: The duration of open-weight price pressure, not just its eventual end, determines damage to US lab economics.
insights.quote: does it not matter tremendously whether that occurs in two months or two years?

themes.theme: Open-weight price compression on US labs

insights.claim: Continued availability of highly capable Chinese open-weight models erodes the moat of American frontier labs, threatening the expected value that lets them, and cloud and neocloud infrastructure providers, raise capital.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Capital access across the US AI buildout, from labs to neoclouds, rests on moat assumptions that Chinese open weights undermine.
insights.quote: it cuts into the moat that American frontier labs currently have, alongside the profits and expected value that this moat would ensure

insights.claim: Industry analyst reporting cited by the author indicates Anthropic's inference margins rose from 38% to 70%, growing alongside revenue.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Frontier inference can be highly profitable; the open question is how much volume cedes to commoditized competitors.
insights.quote: Anthropic’s margins on inference rose from 38% to 70%, growing alongside revenue

insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Upcoming IPOs will expose margin and capex data that will reveal how much open-weight pricing pressure is biting.
insights.quote: As Anthropic prepares its public offering for later this year and OpenAI is set to follow in 2027

insights.claim: A plausible outcome is that machine intelligence becomes too cheap to meter for most usage and commoditized, with large profits only at the frontier edge, forcing US labs to compete on price to remain widely used.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Commoditization would compress lab revenue outside high-complexity workloads, pressuring valuations premised on broad pricing power.
insights.quote: There is a plausible world where machine intelligence becomes too cheap to meter for most usage, too commoditized, yet central to everything.
insights.locator: Dean Ball, Head of Strategic Futures

insights.claim: OpenAI has cut token costs for GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% and Terra by 20%, which the author reads as a possible early sign of price pressure forcing frontier labs to cut prices.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Visible frontier price cuts are a leading indicator of margin compression in model APIs.
insights.quote: OpenAI has already cut token costs for GPT-5.6 Luna by eighty percent and Terra by twenty percent

insights.claim: If China moved away from open-weight models, much value would flow back to US frontier labs, but the longer the price compression lasts, the more damaging it is, making a shift after a year or more far worse for US labs than one within months.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A Chinese policy reversal is a key upside catalyst for US labs whose value decays the longer it is delayed.

themes.theme: Chinese lab monetization and capital efficiency

insights.claim: With Kimi K3's open-weight release, Moonshot AI changed its license so third-party model-as-a-service users earning over $20 million in annual revenue must renegotiate commercial terms, and businesses over 100 million monthly users or that revenue threshold must show Kimi K3 branding.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Chinese labs are finding ways to capture value while staying open-weight, signaling they expect the current regime to persist.

insights.claim: After cutting V4 costs by 75% earlier in 2026, DeepSeek now appears likely to substantially raise API prices.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A DeepSeek price increase would ease some pricing pressure on Western API providers.
insights.quote: after lowering V4 costs by seventy-five percent earlier this year, DeepSeek now seems likely to substantially raise prices for API usage

insights.claim: In a leaked May 20 investor call, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said DeepSeek prices for reasonable profit rather than maximum income, expected its frontier models to remain open-weight, and argued Chinese players will beat US rivals by accepting lower returns.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A competitor explicitly willing to accept lower margins is a structural threat to US lab pricing.
insights.quote: “Those who take more will be beaten by those who take less.”

insights.claim: The leak of Liang Wenfeng's investor call in July disrupted DeepSeek's second fundraising round of the year.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Shows information-leak risk in Chinese AI private financing.

insights.claim: Chinese firms are projected to spend about one-tenth what American firms spend on the AI buildout, suggesting they need far lower profits and capex to thrive.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A 10x capex gap with comparable models implies far better capital efficiency, challenging US capex-heavy return assumptions.
insights.quote: Chinese firms are set to spend about one-tenth the value that American firms will for the AI buildout

insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude valuation gap for labs with comparable capabilities highlights relative value and US valuation risk.
insights.quote: DeepSeek recently raised $7.4 billion at a $50 billion valuation ahead of a possible 2027 IPO on the Shanghai stock exchange

insights.claim: Kai-Fu Lee's 'Moravec's revenge' argument holds that AI automating administrative and service work arrives before intelligent robots, so AI-driven labor disruption would hit America before China.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Suggests US white-collar labor disruption, and resulting political backlash and regulation, may come earlier than in China.
insights.quote: “it’s far easier to build AI algorithms than to build intelligent robots.”

insights.claim: As of 2023, 23% of Chinese workers were in primary agriculture and 29% in manufacturing and industry, while in 2025 43% of the US workforce was in management and professional jobs, 18% in sales and office and 16% in services.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Different workforce compositions imply different political pressure to regulate AI, favoring earlier US restrictions.
insights.quote: As of 2023, 23% of Chinese workers are engaged in primary agriculture and related fields, while another 29% work in manufacturing and industry.

insights.claim: Because government responses to AI are likely driven by short-term job losses, American office workers facing earlier automation could push US governance in a different direction than China's.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Regulatory divergence driven by labor exposure could create asymmetric policy risk for US AI deployment.

insights.claim: In mid-September 2026, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned warning of catastrophic risk, the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI endorsed 'pacing the frontier', a proposal to slow model development.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: A coordinated US frontier slowdown would widen the window for Chinese open-weight catch-up and price competition.

insights.claim: On the same day, September 12, China's Minister of State Security Chen Yixin published an AI article focused on disinformation, cyberattacks, data leaks and military uses, and criticized countries using technology controls, standards monopolies and closed-source ecosystems, without raising job-loss or existential-safety concerns.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Chinese security priorities differ from US safety framing, making a Chinese 'pacing' commitment unlikely.
insights.quote: “implementing technology controls, monopolizing industry standards, and establishing closed-source ecosystems.”

insights.claim: The author hypothesizes China may be uninterested in pacing the frontier because US chip export controls already force it to pace, and may worry less about cyber risk because of its existing cybersecurity state.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Export controls may substitute for voluntary Chinese restraint, shaping how Chinese labs respond to US slowdown proposals.
insights.quote: Perhaps they are uninterested in pacing the frontier because they see America as already forcing them to pace via chip export controls.

insights.claim: The author contends modernity is contingent and that as China prospers, its future innovations and AI governance will take on a distinctly Chinese character rather than converging on Western norms.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Investors should model China as a structurally divergent AI ecosystem, not a lagging copy of the US one.
insights.quote: there is no reason to expect that future innovations will not take on a particularly Chinese character
